title: The communion of saints (CCC 946–962)
hookLine: the living, the dead being purified, and the saints, one family

cards: Walk into an old Catholic church and look up. On the walls, in the windows, painted on the ceiling: faces. Apostles, martyrs, a young nun from Normandy, a Polish priest, a mother, a beggar.
Now look down at the pews: a retired nurse, a kid on a phone, a man who comes every day since his wife died. And somewhere, the Church says, his wife too.
Catholics see the painted faces, the people in the pews and the dead they love as one gathering. There's a line in the Creed that says so.

teach.b: The Apostles' Creed says: I believe in the Holy Ghost, the holy catholic Church, the communion of saints. Catholics say it at the start of the rosary, and promise it again at every baptism.
In Latin it's communio sanctorum, and sanctorum can mean holy people or holy things.
The Catechism says both are true: a sharing in holy things, above all the Eucharist, the sacraments, the faith, and a sharing among holy people.
That one family of God, it says, exists in three states at once. Some are pilgrims on earth. Some have died and are being purified.
And some are in glory, seeing God. Death doesn't cut the family in three. It's one family in three rooms.

The letter to the Hebrews pictures the living as runners in a race, with "so great a cloud of witnesses over our head": the faithful of the chapter before, who bore witness by their lives, now all around the runners.
And Catholics believe love and prayer pass between the rooms in every direction.

teach.h: SO GREAT A CLOUD OF WITNESSES.
teach.b: The saints in heaven pray for those on earth; that's why Catholics ask them for help, the way you'd ask a friend to pray for you. The living pray for the dead who are being purified.
And the good done by any member, the Catechism says, helps all the others.

how: Catholics profess the communion of saints in the Apostles' Creed, ask the saints to pray for them, pray for the dead at every Mass, and keep All Saints on November 1 and All Souls on November 2.

o: a club of people the Church has declared saints
one family of the living, the dead and the saints
a meeting of bishops held in Rome

games.q: what's inside the word — tap the pairs.
p: the living, still on the road
those who have died, not yet whole

s: in Latin, sanctorum can mean holy people or holy things
the Catechism says the communion of saints is both.
Catholics believe death separates the living from the dead completely
the Catechism speaks of one family in three states, joined by love and prayer.
Catholics ask the saints to pray for them the way they'd ask a friend
the saints in glory are believed to intercede for those on earth.

games.q: the Catechism describes the family of God as existing in three states at once. which three?
o: pilgrims on earth, those being purified, and those in glory.
the young, the old, and the unborn.
games.why: one family: pilgrims on earth, the dead being purified, and the saints seeing God.

practice: Bring to mind one person you loved who has died, a grandparent, a friend, a parent, someone you barely knew but think of; say their name quietly and remember one ordinary thing about them, a laugh, a phrase, the way they made coffee.
If you pray, you can pray for them now, in your own words or with the old line, eternal rest grant unto them, O Lord. If you don't, hold them in love for a minute.

wordCard.voice: Communio sanctorum, the Latin behind the communion of saints: a sharing in holy things, and among holy people, living, dead and in glory. Today's word.

orig.note: Latin: the communion of saints, or of holy things. the Creed means both.

carryVoice: Your line: one family. The week ran from dignity to misericordia, soma christou, the four marks, other Christians, other religions, and now a family that death doesn't break. Day three hundred twenty-two: another week, done.
